title: 1 Kings 17:8–16
context: When the brook dries up, the LORD sends Elijah to Zarephath, a town belonging to Sidon, the homeland of Jezebel, where he has commanded a widow to sustain him. The widow is gathering sticks to bake a last meal for herself and her son, yet at Elijah’s word she makes him a cake first, and the jar of meal and the jar of oil do not fail until the rain returns. Jesus later points to this widow as one to whom Elijah was sent, though there were many widows in Israel (Luke 4:25–26). Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the story as shared ground about the LORD’s provision for the needy, his care reaching beyond Israel’s borders, and faith that acts on God’s word. The text presents the meal and oil simply as the LORD keeping his word, and readers in both traditions commonly receive it that way.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to him, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Elijah again just as the brook dries up. God speaks at the point of need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s timely guidance as part of his faithful care. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God does not abandon his servant when circumstances change.

verses.text: “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God sending Elijah to Zarephath in Sidon, Jezebel’s homeland, where he has commanded a widow to sustain him. God’s care reaches beyond Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign choice of an unlikely host, a poor widow outside Israel (compare Luke 4:25–26). Readers in both traditions commonly see God’s concern for widows reflected here (compare Psalm 68:5).

verses.text: So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her and said, “Please get me a little water in a jar, that I may drink.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah arriving at the city gate and finding the widow gathering sticks. He asks her for a little water, beginning with a modest request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting as arranged by God’s providence. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the start of a story in which faith grows through small steps of obedience.

verses.text: As she was going to get it, he called to her and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah also asking for a morsel of bread. The request tests the widow’s willingness to share in a time of famine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as preparing to reveal God’s provision through her. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a costly invitation to trust.

verses.text: She said, “As the LORD your God lives, I don’t have anything baked, but only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and bake it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the widow’s honest reply that she has only a handful of meal and a little oil, planning a last meal before death. Her despair is real and moving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that she swears by the LORD your God, recognizing Elijah’s God though she is a Sidonian. Both traditions commonly read the verse with compassion for her desperate situation.

verses.text: Elijah said to her, “Don’t be afraid. Go and do as you have said; but make me a little cake from it first, and bring it out to me, and afterward make some for you and for your son.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah telling her not to be afraid and to make him a cake first. God’s word calls for faith before the provision is seen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s request as grounded in the promise that follows. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as inviting trust in God’s word over visible scarcity.

verses.text: For the LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘The jar of meal will not run out, and the jar of oil will not fail, until the day that the LORD sends rain on the earth.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s promise that the meal and oil will not fail until rain returns. The word of God gives the widow reason to act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise as a sure word from the LORD, the God of Israel. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s provision rests on his faithfulness.

verses.text: She went and did according to the saying of Elijah; and she, he, and her household ate many days.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the widow doing according to Elijah’s word, and her household eating many days. Her faith responds freely to God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her obedience as faith that God has worked in her. Readers in both traditions commonly honor her trust as a striking example of faith in a Gentile.

verses.text: The jar of meal didn’t run out and the jar of oil didn’t fail, according to the LORD’s word, which he spoke by Elijah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the jar of meal and oil not failing, according to the LORD’s word by Elijah. God keeps his promise exactly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s faithfulness to his word as the point of the miracle. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s provision, without pressing further symbolism (compare Philippians 4:19).
